The Levites are described again as “a gift” to the priests, and remarkably, the priesthood itself is called “a gift” God gives: “I give your priesthood as a gift.” Calvin observes the grace embedded in this language; the priesthood is not a human achievement or right but a divine gift, freely bestowed. Sproul reflected that all true ministry is a gift of God, never a possession to be seized — the very lesson Korah failed to learn. The repeated warning, “any outsider who comes near shall be put to death,” preserves the seriousness of the appointed mediation. But the dominant note is grace: God gives the Levites, gives the priesthood, gives the means by which his people may safely draw near. The whole arrangement is a gift designed to make a way for sinful people to live in the presence of a holy God. And it all anticipates the supreme gift — the Father who “gave his only Son” (John 3:16), the great High Priest given to guard us forever from wrath, so that for those in Christ “there is therefore now no condemnation” (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — The Provision for the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests are supported by the offerings, firstfruits, and devoted things of the people — their portion from the LORD’s table.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who serve at the altar live from the altar; God provides for his ministers through the gifts of his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests fed from the offerings. Now: those who preach the gospel live from the gospel, as God provides for his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: “Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, ‘Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due... Every offering of theirs, every grain offering... that they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons. ... Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Having no land of their own, the priests are provided for from the offerings of the people — “I have given you charge of the contributions made to me... as a portion.” Wenham notes the principle; the priests live from the very gifts the people bring to God. What is offered to the LORD becomes the sustenance of those who minister at his altar. Calvin observes the fittingness of this arrangement; those who devote themselves wholly to the service of the sanctuary, owning no fields, are sustained by the worship they facilitate. The portions are called “most holy,” to be eaten in reverence by the clean of the priestly household. Sproul reflected on the enduring principle that Paul draws from this very arrangement; “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Cor 9:14), and “the laborer deserves his wages” (1 Tim 5:18). God ordains that his ministers be supported by his people, freed from the need to provide for themselves so they may give themselves to the work. There is dignity in this; the priests do not beg but receive what God himself has assigned them from his own table. The provision is generous and abundant, drawn from the firstfruits, the offerings, and the consecrated things. And it teaches a gospel principle still binding on the church — that God’s people are to support those who minister the word and sacraments among them, sharing their material good with those who serve them spiritually.

verseByVerse.quote: “‘Everything that opens the womb of all flesh... shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem... All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you. ... It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you.’”
verseByVerse.commentary: The provision continues with the firstborn and the firstfruits — “all the best of the oil and... wine and... grain.” Wenham notes that God gives his ministers not the leftovers but “the best,” the firstfruits, the choicest portion. The God who deserves the best gives the best to those who serve him. The redemption of the firstborn of man (recalling ch 3) is woven in, the price paid to the priests. Calvin observes the generosity of God toward his servants; he does not stint but provides abundantly from the finest of the land’s produce. The arrangement is sealed as “a covenant of salt forever” — salt being the symbol of permanence, preservation, and an unbreakable bond (cf. 2 Chron 13:5). Sproul reflected on the beauty of the “covenant of salt”; God binds himself by an enduring covenant to provide for his priests, a pledge as lasting and incorruptible as salt itself. There is deep assurance in this for all who serve God; he commits himself faithfully to their care. The phrase points beyond itself to the permanence of God’s covenant faithfulness. And the giving of “the best” to the priests teaches a heart-principle for all worship; we are to give God, and those who serve him, not our scraps but our finest. The covenant of salt, unbreakable and preserving, foreshadows the new and better covenant established in the blood of Christ, by which God binds himself forever to provide for and preserve his people, who are themselves “the salt of the earth” (Matt 5:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — ‘I Am Your Portion’ and the Levites’ Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests receive no land, for the LORD himself is their portion; the Levites receive the tithe and in turn tithe to the priests.
verseByVerse.theology: To have God himself as one’s inheritance is the highest treasure; the landless tribe possesses the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priests’ portion is the LORD himself. Now: in Christ, God himself is the believer’s inheritance forever.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD said to Aaron, ‘You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel. To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service that they do, their service in the tent of meeting...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the crown jewel of the chapter, one of the great treasures of all Scripture: “I am your portion and your inheritance.” Wenham notes the stunning exchange; the priests receive no allotment of land — no fields, no vineyards, no territory — because they have something infinitely greater. They have God himself. The tribe that owns no earth possesses the LORD of heaven. Calvin observes that this is the highest privilege imaginable; while the other tribes inherit portions of Canaan, the priests inherit God, and surely the Giver is greater than all his gifts. Sproul reflected with deep feeling on this verse; to have God as one’s portion is to be richer than all the landed tribes combined, for what is the land compared to the One who made it? Keller often returned to this theme — that the gospel offers not merely God’s gifts but God himself, and that the soul which has God lacks nothing. Asaph would later make this his song in the darkest hour: “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Ps 73:26). The Levites receive the tithe as their inheritance, but the priests receive the LORD. And the New Testament makes this the inheritance of every believer; in Christ we are made “a kingdom, priests to his God” (Rev 1:6), and our portion is God himself — “the LORD is my chosen portion” (Ps 16:5). To possess God is to possess everything; the landless priest, with God as his portion, was the richest man in Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: “And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Moreover, you shall speak and say to the Levites, When you take from the people of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall present a contribution from it to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe... And you shall say to them, “When you have offered from it the best of it, then the rest shall be counted to the Levites...” And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it...’”
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the Levites, who receive the tithe, must themselves tithe — presenting “a tithe of the tithe,” the best of what they receive, back to the LORD through the priests. Wenham notes the principle that no one in Israel, not even the ministers, is exempt from giving God his portion; all that we receive is first to be acknowledged as God’s by returning the best to him. Calvin observes the fittingness of this; those who live by the gifts of God’s people must themselves honor God with the firstfruits of what they receive. The Levites give “the best of it,” not the inferior remainder — the same principle that governed the priests’ portion. Sproul reflected that this teaches the universal duty of grateful giving; even those who minister and are supported by others are called to give back to God, for all giving flows from the prior recognition that everything is his. There is a beautiful order in the economy of God’s house; the people give to the Levites, the Levites give to the priests, and the priests offer to the LORD — a chain of grateful acknowledgment that all belongs to God. The assurance “you shall bear no sin... when you have contributed the best” promises that faithful giving brings not loss but blessing and a clear conscience. The whole arrangement teaches that the people of God, at every level, live by receiving from God and returning to him the best, in glad acknowledgment that he is the source and owner of all, and that, in the end, he himself is our true and everlasting portion.

18.theology:
The Mediators Bear the Danger of Holiness. Answering the people’s cry, “Are we all to perish?”, the priests “bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary,” guarding it so that wrath may not fall on the people. This substitutionary bearing points to Christ, who bore our sins in his body, taking the full danger of holiness upon himself.

Those Who Serve the Altar Live from the Altar. The priests and Levites, having no land, are supported by the offerings and the best of the produce, sealed by a covenant of salt. Paul applies this to gospel ministry: those who preach the gospel should live by the gospel; God’s people support those who serve them spiritually.

God Himself the Portion. “I am your portion and your inheritance.” The landless priests possess the LORD, and so are richer than all the landed tribes. In Christ this becomes the inheritance of every believer — not merely God’s gifts but God himself, our chosen portion forever.
18.examples:
Then: The priests bore the danger of the sanctuary so that wrath would not fall on the people, were sustained by the offerings, and received not land but the LORD himself as their portion.

Now: Christ, your great High Priest, has borne the danger of holiness and the weight of your sin, so you may draw near and live. Support those who minister God’s word among you. And treasure your true inheritance: not merely God’s gifts, but God himself. With Asaph, say, “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”

19.title: The Red Heifer: The Paradox of Purification
19.text: <sup>2</sup>This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Tell the people of Israel to bring you a red heifer without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which a yoke has never come. <sup>9</sup>...And the ashes shall be kept for the water for impurity, for the removal of sin.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 gives one of the strangest and most profound rituals in the law: the red heifer. An unblemished red cow, never yoked, is slaughtered outside the camp, burned entirely, and its ashes mixed with water to make the “water for impurity.” This water cleanses anyone defiled by contact with death. In a wilderness where a whole generation is dying, the need is constant; death contaminates, and the people must be made clean to remain in the presence of the living God.

The ritual is full of paradox, which the rabbis themselves found baffling. The ashes that purify the unclean also defile the clean: the priest who prepares them becomes unclean. The very thing that cleanses the defiled defiles the clean. Wenham notes that this strange reversal dramatizes the deep mystery of how cleansing from death is achieved — at a cost, by something that absorbs the defilement. The means of cleansing bears the uncleanness it removes.

The book of Hebrews seizes on this exact ritual: “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ… purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb 9:13–14). The red heifer purified the outside; Christ purifies the conscience. The heifer was burned outside the camp; Christ suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:12). The ashes that bore defilement to bring cleansing are a shadow of the One who “became sin” for us (2 Cor 5:21), absorbing our death-defilement into himself that we might be made clean. The red heifer asks the question; the cross of Christ is the answer.

sections.title: The Red Heifer Slaughtered
sections.commentary:
An unblemished red heifer that has never borne a yoke is led outside the camp and slaughtered, its blood sprinkled toward the tent of meeting, and the whole animal burned with cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet yarn. The ashes are gathered and kept for the water of purification. Sproul noted the careful specifications: unblemished, never yoked, wholly given. Every detail points to a perfect, unused, fully consecrated victim, a shadow of the spotless Lamb who had never been bound by sin's yoke.

Crucially, the heifer is killed and burned outside the camp. Hebrews makes the connection explicit: Jesus also suffered outside the gate, bearing reproach, to sanctify the people by his own blood (Heb 13:11–13). The place of the heifer's death is the place of Christ's death, where the defiled find their cleansing.

sections.title: The Water for Impurity
sections.commentary:
Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days and must be purified with the water made from the heifer's ashes, or be cut off from Israel for defiling the tabernacle of the LORD. Death is the great defiler, the wage of sin (Rom 6:23), and in a camp full of dying it threatened the people's standing before the living God. Ferguson observes that the constant need for this cleansing preached a constant sermon: death contaminates, and only a God-appointed means can remove its stain.

The provision is mercy. God does not leave the death-defiled in their uncleanness but supplies a way to be made clean and remain near him. So Christ does not leave us in the contamination of our sin and death but cleanses us by his blood.

sections.title: The Application of the Ashes
sections.commentary:
Detailed laws govern the defilement of tents, open vessels, and those who touch the slain or the dead. On the third and seventh days a clean person sprinkles the water of purification on the unclean, who washes and is clean by evening. The repeated sprinkling underscores that cleansing is not automatic but applied; the provision must be received. Begg notes that the ashes did no good sitting in a jar; they had to be applied to the defiled. So the blood of Christ, sufficient for all, cleanses those to whom it is applied by faith.

The clean person who sprinkles makes the cleansing possible for others, a quiet picture of the ministry of the gospel, by which the cleansing of Christ is applied to the defiled.

sections.title: The Paradox of Cleansing
sections.commentary:
Here is the great mystery: the one who prepares and handles the purifying ashes becomes himself unclean, while the ashes cleanse the defiled. The thing that purifies the unclean defiles the clean. Wenham calls this the central paradox of the chapter, and it dramatizes substitution: the means of cleansing absorbs the defilement it removes.

This is the gospel in shadow. Christ, the clean and spotless One, was made unclean with our defilement; he who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Cor 5:21). The cleanser took the contamination. By becoming unclean in our place, he made the unclean clean. The red heifer poses the riddle that only the cross can answer: how can the defiled be purified? By One who bears their defilement away.

19.theology:
Death and defilement. Death is the great contaminator, the wage of sin. The red heifer provides cleansing from death's stain so the people may remain near the living God.

The paradox of substitution. The ashes that cleanse the defiled defile the clean. The means of purification bears the uncleanness it removes, a shadow of Christ who became sin for us.

Cleansing of the conscience. The heifer purified the flesh; the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb 9:13–14).
19.examples:
Then: A red heifer was burned outside the camp, and its ashes made water that cleansed the death-defiled, while the one who prepared it became unclean himself.

Now: Christ suffered outside the gate, became unclean with your defilement, and by his blood purifies not merely the flesh but the conscience. The riddle of the red heifer is answered at the cross; come and be clean.

20.title: Water from the Rock; the Death of Aaron: When the Mediator Fails
20.text: <sup>10</sup>and Moses said to them, Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock? <sup>11</sup>And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly. <sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 marks the beginning of the end of the wilderness generation, and it is heavy with loss. Miriam dies. Aaron dies. And Moses commits the sin that will bar him from the Promised Land. The chapter opens at Kadesh, where the people once again have no water and once again grumble, exactly as their parents had done. The cycle of unbelief repeats in the new generation. But the tragedy here belongs not to the people but to Moses.

God commands Moses to speak to the rock, and it will give water. But Moses, exasperated and angry, addresses the people as “you rebels,” takes the glory to himself (“shall we bring water?”), and strikes the rock — twice — instead of speaking to it. The water gushes out; God is gracious to the thirsty people. But God's verdict on Moses is severe: “Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy… you shall not bring this assembly into the land.” The meekest man on earth, the great intercessor, will die outside Canaan. Sproul observed that the severity of the judgment matches the privilege of the man: to whom much is given, much is required, and Moses had misrepresented the holiness of God before the people.

Paul tells us what was truly at stake: “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4). The rock struck for water is a figure of Christ smitten for us, from whom flow the living waters of salvation. At the first rock (Exod 17) Moses was told to strike, and Christ was indeed struck once for sin. But this second time Moses was told only to speak, for the smitten Rock need not be struck again; Christ “was offered once to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28). By striking the rock a second time, Moses marred the picture of the gospel — and that is why the judgment was so grave. Yet even Moses' failure magnifies the perfection of the true Mediator, who never failed to uphold the holiness of God, and who alone could lead his people into the rest Moses could not enter.

sections.title: The Death of Miriam and the People's Thirst
sections.commentary:
Israel comes to Kadesh, where Miriam dies and is buried. Again there is no water, and again the people quarrel with Moses, rehearsing the old complaint: better to have died, why bring us to this evil place? The new generation has inherited the old generation's grumbling heart. Ferguson notes how sobering this is: the children repeat the sins of the parents, proving that unbelief is not cured by mere change of personnel but only by a change of heart.

Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the LORD, and the glory of the LORD appears. As ever, the mediators turn to God in the people's crisis. The pattern is right, even as the sequel will go wrong.

sections.title: Moses Strikes the Rock
sections.commentary:
God tells Moses to take the staff and speak to the rock so that it yields water. But Moses, provoked, calls the people “rebels,” asks “shall we bring water out of this rock?”, and strikes the rock twice. Water gushes out abundantly. God's grace to the thirsty people is undiminished even by his servant's sin; the water flows. Calvin notes the mingling of divine faithfulness and human failure: God keeps his promise to the people while holding his servant accountable.

Three faults converge in Moses: anger that misrepresents God's heart, pride that claims the glory (“shall we”), and disobedience that strikes when told to speak. Begg notes the danger of ministry done in the flesh; even a great servant can, in a moment of unbelief, distort the God he represents.

sections.title: The Sentence on Moses and Aaron
sections.commentary:
God's verdict is grave: “Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land.” The waters are named Meribah, “quarreling.” Sproul stressed that the sin was unbelief expressed as a failure to treat God as holy before the people. Leaders represent God; to misrepresent him is no small thing.

And yet, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4). The first rock was struck once (Exod 17); this one was only to be spoken to, for the Rock smitten once for sin need not be struck again. By striking twice, Moses marred the gospel picture: Christ was offered once for all (Heb 9:28). The severity of the judgment guards the truth that our Mediator's one sacrifice is final and sufficient.

sections.title: Edom's Refusal and the Death of Aaron
sections.commentary:
Edom refuses Israel passage, and they must turn aside. Then, at Mount Hor, Aaron's priestly garments are transferred to his son Eleazar, and Aaron dies on the mountain. The first high priest of Israel dies outside the Promised Land, and all the congregation mourns him thirty days. Wenham notes the poignancy: the priesthood continues, the garments pass to the next generation, but the man himself dies in the wilderness under the sentence on his unbelief.

Here is the great limitation of the old order. Aaron, like every mortal priest, dies and must hand on his office. Hebrews draws the contrast: the Levitical priests were many “because they were prevented by death from continuing in office,” but Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Heb 7:23–24). Aaron's death on the mountain magnifies the undying priesthood of the One who lives forever to save.

20.theology:
The smitten Rock. The rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4), struck once for sin. Moses' striking it a second time marred the gospel picture, for Christ was offered once for all (Heb 9:28).

The holiness of God in leadership. Moses failed to uphold God as holy before the people. Those who represent God bear a weighty responsibility not to misrepresent his character.

The mortal priesthood. Aaron dies outside the land, his office passed on. The dying priests of the old order magnify the undying priesthood of Christ who lives forever.
20.examples:
Then: The people grumbled for water, Moses struck the rock in anger and was barred from the land, and Aaron died on Mount Hor, his priesthood passing to his son.

Now: The Rock has been struck once for you; he need not be struck again, for Christ was offered once for all. Drink freely of the living water that flows from the smitten Savior, and follow the Priest who never fails and never dies.

21.title: The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
21.text: <sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live. <sup>9</sup>So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 contains the brightest gospel light in the whole book of Numbers, for our Lord himself pointed to it: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The people grumble yet again — “there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food” (the manna!) — and God sends fiery serpents among them, and many die. The judgment fits the sin: a people who spit venom at God are bitten by venom.

The people repent and cry out, and God gives a remedy so strange and so glorious that it can only be the gospel. He does not remove the serpents. He commands Moses to make a bronze serpent and lift it up on a pole, and “everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” The cure is not in medicine or effort but in a look. The dying are not told to fight the serpents, or to climb the pole, or to be worthy — only to look. Keller observed that this is salvation by faith alone in its purest Old Testament form: not by doing, but by looking away from yourself to the thing God has provided. The simplest, weakest, most desperate look saves.

And what was lifted up? An image of the very thing that was killing them — a serpent, the curse itself, raised on a pole. Ferguson marvels at the depth of this: on the cross, God lifted up his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom 8:3), made him to be sin and a curse for us (2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13). The serpent, the symbol of the curse since Eden, was lifted up so that all who looked might live. So Christ became the curse, lifted up on the pole of the cross, and every sin-bitten, dying sinner who looks to him in faith — not by working, only by looking — shall live. “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isa 45:22). This is the heart of the gospel, hidden in the heart of Numbers.

sections.title: Victory at Hormah and Renewed Grumbling
sections.commentary:
Israel defeats the Canaanite king of Arad after vowing devotion to the LORD, a foretaste of conquest. But on the long way around Edom, the people become impatient and speak against God and Moses, complaining of no food and no water and loathing “this worthless food,” the manna. Begg notes the staggering ingratitude of calling the bread of heaven worthless. The new generation's heart is no better than the old; grumbling against grace is the perennial human disease.

The contrast is sharp: a fresh victory granted by God, immediately followed by fresh contempt for God's provision. Such is the human heart, quick to forget the latest mercy and despise the daily bread.

sections.title: The Fiery Serpents
sections.commentary:
God sends fiery serpents among the people, and many die. The judgment fits the crime: a people whose words spit venom against God are bitten by venomous serpents. Sproul noted that God's judgments often hold up a mirror to the sin. The people then come to Moses confessing, “We have sinned… pray that the LORD take away the serpents,” and Moses intercedes once more for the people who had just maligned him.

The confession is genuine and the cry for mediation is right. Yet notice that God's answer will not be the removal of the serpents but the provision of a remedy. The curse remains in the world; God provides a way to live in the midst of it.

sections.title: The Bronze Serpent Lifted Up
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole; whoever is bitten and looks at it shall live. The cure is by sight, by faith, not by effort. The dying need only look. Keller called this the purest picture of justification by faith in the Old Testament: salvation comes not by what we do but by looking to what God has provided.

Jesus claimed this text as his own: “As Moses lifted up the serpent… so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14–15). The serpent, emblem of the curse, was lifted on a pole so that the cursed might live by looking. So Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), lifted up on the cross, and every sin-bitten sinner who looks to him in faith shall not perish but have eternal life.

sections.title: Songs, Wells, and Victories over Sihon and Og
sections.commentary:
Israel journeys on, singing at the well God provides (“Spring up, O well!”), and then defeats Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, taking their lands. The mood has shifted from grumbling to song, from death to victory. Wenham notes the turning: as the wilderness years end, God begins to give visible victories, foretastes of the conquest of the land.

These triumphs over Sihon and Og are remembered throughout Scripture as signal demonstrations of God's power to give his people their inheritance (Ps 135–136). The God who provides the bronze serpent for the bitten also goes before his people to conquer. Salvation and victory both come from his hand, and the same Lord who saves us by a look also fights for us and brings us home.

21.theology:
Look and live. The bronze serpent saves by sight, not effort — the purest Old Testament picture of justification by faith. Christ lifted up saves all who simply look to him (John 3:14–15).

The curse lifted up. The serpent, emblem of the curse, was raised on a pole. So Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), bearing the very judgment that was killing us.

Judgment that fits the sin. Venomous words met venomous serpents. God's judgments hold up a mirror, yet his mercy provides a remedy in the midst of the curse.
21.examples:
Then: God sent fiery serpents for Israel's grumbling, then provided a bronze serpent on a pole, so that everyone bitten who looked at it would live.

Now: You have been bitten by the serpent of sin and are dying. Do not look to yourself, your works, or your worthiness. Look to Christ lifted up on the cross, who became the curse for you, and live. The weakest look of faith saves.

22.title: Balak and Balaam: The Sovereign God over a Pagan Prophet
22.text: <sup>12</sup>God said to Balaam, You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed. <sup>28</sup>Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?
22.overview:
With chapters 22–24 the narrative pulls back to show us something Israel could not see: while they camp on the plains of Moab, unaware, a spiritual battle is being waged over their destiny. Balak king of Moab, terrified of Israel, hires the renowned pagan seer Balaam to curse them. The drama that unfolds is one of the most remarkable demonstrations of God's sovereignty in all of Scripture, for God will so overrule this hireling prophet that Balaam cannot speak anything but blessing over the people God has blessed.

The famous episode of the talking donkey is not comic relief but theology in story form. Balaam, the celebrated seer who claims to see what others cannot, is blind to the angel of the LORD standing in his path with a drawn sword — while his donkey sees plainly. The prophet who boasts of open eyes is more blind than his beast. Calvin and others note the biting irony: God humbles the proud seer by speaking through a donkey and by giving sight to an animal that he withholds from the man. The God who can open a donkey's mouth can open or shut any mouth he pleases.

Here is the deep comfort of the chapter: the people of God are surrounded by enemies who plot their ruin, and they do not even know it — yet God is in complete control of the plot. “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed” (Isa 54:17). Ferguson notes that Balaam is the picture of every enemy of the church: God holds even the curses of the wicked in his hand and turns them to blessing. Romans 8 stands over this chapter: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” The God who would not let Balaam curse his people is the God who works all things, even the schemes of his enemies, for the good of those he has blessed in Christ.

sections.title: Balak's Fear and First Summons
sections.commentary:
Balak king of Moab, dreading the multitude of Israel, sends elders with fees for divination to summon Balaam to curse them. Balaam inquires of God, who flatly forbids him: “You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed.” Sproul noted the finality of this divine word; the blessing of God on his people is not subject to reversal by any sorcerer. Balaam reports that God will not let him go, and the first delegation returns empty-handed.

From the outset the verdict is settled in heaven. Whatever maneuvering follows on earth, the people God has blessed cannot be cursed. The whole episode is a dramatization of the security of those whom God has set his love upon.

sections.title: The Second Summons and Balaam's Compromise
sections.commentary:
Balak sends more honorable princes and greater rewards. Balaam protests that he cannot go beyond the word of the LORD even for a house full of silver and gold, yet he asks God again, hoping for a different answer. God permits him to go but only to speak what God commands. Begg notes the divided heart of Balaam: his lips honor God while his heart hankers after the reward. He is the very type of the double-minded man, religious in speech but mercenary at the core, “who loved gain from wrongdoing” (2 Pet 2:15).

Balaam's repeated asking, when God had already spoken, exposes a heart that wants the wages more than the will of God. He goes, technically permitted, but with a covetous heart that the next scene will expose.

sections.title: The Donkey and the Angel
sections.commentary:
God's anger is kindled, and the angel of the LORD stands in the road with a drawn sword. The donkey sees the angel three times and turns aside, but Balaam, blind, beats her — until the LORD opens the donkey's mouth to rebuke him, and then opens Balaam's eyes to see the angel. The renowned seer is more blind than his beast. Calvin relished the irony: God humbles the proud prophet through a donkey, exposing that all true sight is God's gift.

The angel warns that the donkey saved Balaam's life by turning aside, and that Balaam may go only to speak God's words. Wenham notes the lesson in sovereignty: God controls not only what Balaam will say but whether he lives to say it. The whole apparatus of pagan divination is helpless before the living God.

sections.title: Balaam Meets Balak
sections.commentary:
Balak meets Balaam with reproach for his delay, and Balaam warns him plainly: “The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak.” Balak takes him up to a high place to look upon the people he hopes to curse. The stage is set for the oracles. Ferguson notes the dramatic irony hanging over the scene: Balak has paid a fortune to curse Israel, and the curse will come out as blessing every time.

The chapter closes with the king of Moab and the hireling seer poised on a mountaintop, plotting against the people of God, while heaven has already decreed that only blessing will fall. Here is the security of the elect: their enemies may scheme on the heights, but God has spoken, and his people are blessed.

22.theology:
Sovereignty over enemies. God so controls the pagan Balaam that he cannot curse the people God has blessed. No weapon fashioned against God's people shall prosper.

The security of the blessed. They are blessed, and the blessing of God cannot be reversed by any curse. If God is for us, who can be against us (Rom 8:31)?

God humbles the proud. The seer is blinder than his donkey; all true sight is God's gift. The Lord can open a beast's mouth and shut a prophet's, as he pleases.
22.examples:
Then: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God forbade the curse, opened a donkey's mouth to rebuke the blind seer, and decreed that only blessing would fall.

Now: You are surrounded by enemies you cannot see, who plot against you — yet God holds their curses in his hand and turns them to blessing. Those whom God has blessed in Christ cannot be cursed. Rest in the sovereign Lord who is for you.

23.title: Balaam's First and Second Oracles: God Is Not Man, That He Should Lie
23.text: <sup>19</sup>God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it? <sup>20</sup>Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it.
23.overview:
Balak builds altars and offers sacrifices, again and again, trying to manipulate the spiritual machinery into producing a curse. But every time Balaam opens his mouth, blessing pours out. The first two oracles of Balaam are among the most magnificent declarations of God's unbreakable purpose for his people anywhere in Scripture. The pagan prophet, against his own financial interest and his employer's furious demands, can only say what God puts in his mouth.

The first oracle marvels that Israel is a people set apart, “dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations,” innumerable as the dust — the Abrahamic promise confirmed by an enemy's mouth. The second oracle rises even higher to the bedrock truth of verse 19: “God is not man, that he should lie… Has he said, and will he not do it?” Sproul called this one of the supreme statements of divine immutability and faithfulness in all of Scripture. God does not change his mind, does not lie, does not break his word. What he has promised, he will perform. The blessing he has spoken over his people cannot be revoked, because the God who spoke it cannot lie.

And then comes the staggering declaration: “He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel” (v. 21). How can God say this of the very people who have grumbled, rebelled, and died by the thousands in the wilderness? Ferguson points to the mystery and glory of imputation: God looks on his covenant people not according to their sin but according to his covenant grace. He sees them as righteous because of his own commitment to them. Here, faintly but truly, is the doctrine of justification — God declaring his people blameless not because they are, but because he has covered them. The full answer comes only in Christ, in whom God sees no condemnation (Rom 8:1), having laid our sin on his Son and clothed us in his righteousness. The curse cannot land, for God beholds his people in his Beloved.

sections.title: The First Sacrifice and Oracle
sections.commentary:
Balaam has seven altars built and offers bulls and rams, then receives God's word. His first oracle confesses he cannot curse whom God has not cursed: Israel dwells alone, a distinct people, numerous as the dust, and Balaam even longs to “die the death of the upright.” Balak is furious: “I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them.” Calvin notes the comedy of frustrated wickedness; all Balak's altars and fees cannot extract a single curse.

The oracle celebrates Israel's separateness and innumerability, the very promises made to Abraham, now confirmed by the mouth of a hostile seer. God will use even his enemies to proclaim the security of his people.

sections.title: God's Unchanging Word
sections.commentary:
Balak tries a new vantage point and more sacrifices, but the second oracle opens with the towering truth: “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it?” Sproul treasured this as a pillar of God's immutability and faithfulness. Unlike fickle, lying humanity, God's word is sure; what he has spoken he will perform.

Therefore, Balaam confesses, “I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it.” The blessing is irrevocable because the Blesser is unchangeable. Begg notes the comfort: our security rests not on our constancy but on God's, and his word cannot fail. Every promise of God finds its Yes in Christ (2 Cor 1:20).

sections.title: No Misfortune Beheld in Jacob
sections.commentary:
“He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them.” The wonder is overwhelming: God says he sees no iniquity in the people who have rebelled at every turn. Ferguson points to the deep logic of covenant grace and imputation: God beholds his people not in their sin but in his gracious commitment to them.

This is justification in shadow. God declares his people blameless not because they are, but because he has set his love on them and will cover their sin. The full answer is Christ, in whom “there is therefore now no condemnation” (Rom 8:1). God sees no charge against his people because their sin was laid on his Son.

sections.title: Balak's Frustration
sections.commentary:
Balak, exasperated, cries, “Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all!” But even his attempt to silence Balaam fails; the seer reminds him again that he must speak only what God says. Undeterred, Balak drags him to yet another high place to try once more. Wenham notes the mounting irony: each new mountain yields only more blessing, and the king's rage only magnifies God's sovereign control.

The repeated, futile maneuvering preaches a sermon: the enemies of God's people exhaust themselves in vain. The blessing of God cannot be cancelled, redirected, or silenced. What God has decreed for those he loves stands immovable against every scheme.

23.theology:
God's immutability and faithfulness. God is not man, that he should lie or change his mind. What he has promised, he will perform; his blessing cannot be revoked.

Imputed blamelessness. God beholds no iniquity in Jacob, not because they are sinless, but because of covenant grace, anticipating justification in Christ in whom there is no condemnation.

The futility of opposition. Every altar and high place fails to produce a curse. The enemies of God's people exhaust themselves in vain against an unchangeable decree.
23.examples:
Then: Balak built altars and demanded curses, but God turned every oracle into blessing, declaring himself unchangeable and beholding no iniquity in his people.

Now: The God who cannot lie has spoken his blessing over you in Christ, and it cannot be revoked. He beholds no condemnation in those covered by his Son. Rest in promises that are Yes and Amen in Jesus, sealed by a God who does not change.

24.title: Balaam's Final Oracles: A Star Shall Come Out of Jacob
24.text: <sup>17</sup>I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.
24.overview:
The Balaam saga reaches its glorious climax. By now Balaam no longer even resorts to omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and his eyes are opened. The third oracle pours out a vision of Israel's beauty and flourishing — “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!” (v. 5) — words still sung at the door of synagogues to this day. The hireling who came to curse stands transfixed by the loveliness of the people of God.

But the fourth oracle soars highest of all, into outright Messianic prophecy. “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (v. 17). Balaam sees, across the centuries, the coming of a King — a royal Star, a ruling Scepter — who will arise from Israel and triumph over all her enemies. Sproul and others have long understood this as one of the great Old Testament Messianic prophecies, looking forward to the King who would come from Jacob's line. When the magi from the East followed a star to Bethlehem to worship the newborn King of the Jews (Matt 2), many have heard the echo of Balaam's ancient oracle: the Star out of Jacob had risen at last.

The wonder is who speaks this prophecy: not a faithful Israelite but a pagan, mercenary seer, overruled by the Spirit of God to proclaim the coming of the Messiah. Ferguson notes the sovereign freedom of God, who can put the gospel of the coming King even in the mouth of his enemy. The God who would not let Balaam curse his people compelled him instead to prophesy the King who would save them. And so the deepest comfort of the whole Balaam narrative arrives: the security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King. The Star has risen; the Scepter has been raised; and the Lord Jesus reigns over all who would oppose his people, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev 19:16).

sections.title: The Third Oracle: The Loveliness of Israel
sections.commentary:
Balaam no longer seeks omens; the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he sees Israel encamped tribe by tribe. He bursts out, “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob!” and pictures Israel as well-watered gardens, lofty cedars, a lion that none dares rouse. He closes with the Abrahamic blessing: “Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you” (cf. Gen 12:3). Begg notes the irony of the curse-for-hire becoming a benediction; God turns the intended curse into the patriarchal blessing itself.

The pagan seer, overcome by the Spirit, beholds the beauty of the people of God. So one day every enemy will confess the loveliness of the church Christ has cleansed and made glorious.

sections.title: Balak's Fury and Balaam's Boldness
sections.commentary:
Balak's anger boils over; he strikes his hands together and dismisses Balaam without reward. But Balaam, before leaving, insists once more that he could not go beyond the word of the LORD even for a house of silver and gold, and announces a final word about what Israel will do to Moab in days to come. Wenham notes the mounting drama: the rejected prophet now delivers, unbidden, the greatest oracle of all.

The loss of his fee cannot stop the word of God; indeed, the very rejection becomes the occasion for the climactic Messianic prophecy. God's purposes advance even through the frustration of his enemies.

sections.title: The Star Out of Jacob
sections.commentary:
The fourth oracle rises to Messianic glory: “A star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.” Balaam sees a coming King, “but not now… not near,” a royal figure from Jacob's line who will triumph over Moab and all enemies. Sproul affirmed this as a great Messianic prophecy, pointing across the centuries to the King who would come from Israel.

The Star and Scepter are royal images of dominion. Many have linked the magi's star (Matt 2) to this very oracle: the Star out of Jacob rose over Bethlehem, and the King foretold by a pagan seer came to reign. The security of God's people rests at last on the coming of God's King, who is Christ the Lord, King of kings forever.

sections.title: Oracles Against the Nations
sections.commentary:
Balaam pronounces further oracles against Amalek, the Kenites, and other nations, foreseeing their downfall, and then rises and returns home. The sweep of these final words shows the Star-King's dominion extending over all the nations that oppose God's people. Ferguson notes the universal reach: the coming King will not merely deliver Israel but rule over the peoples.

The Balaam narrative ends with the kingdom of God in view, the Messiah's triumph over every hostile power. The God who would not let his people be cursed has revealed the King through whom every enemy will be subdued. The whole episode closes pointing forward to Christ's universal reign.

24.theology:
The Star out of Jacob. Balaam prophesies a coming royal King from Israel, a great Messianic oracle fulfilled in Christ, the Star and Scepter, whose star rose over Bethlehem.

God's sovereign freedom. God overrules even a pagan, mercenary prophet to proclaim the coming Messiah. He can put the gospel in the mouth of his enemy.

The King secures his people. The security of God's people rests on the coming of God's King, who reigns over every hostile nation as King of kings and Lord of lords.
24.examples:
Then: The Spirit overcame Balaam, who beheld the loveliness of Israel and prophesied a Star out of Jacob, a coming King who would crush every enemy.

Now: The Star has risen. The King foretold by a pagan seer has come, and he reigns. Your security rests not in yourself but in Christ the Scepter of Israel, before whom every enemy will bow and every curse be turned to blessing.

25.title: Baal of Peor: The Seduction Balaam's Curse Could Not Achieve
25.text: <sup>1</sup>While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab. <sup>11</sup>Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy.
25.overview:
What Balaam could not accomplish by cursing, he accomplished by seduction. Numbers 31:16 reveals that Balaam, unable to curse Israel, counseled Balak to corrupt them — to lure them into sexual immorality and idolatry with the women of Moab. And it works where the curse failed. The enemy who cannot defeat the people of God from outside seeks to destroy them from within, through compromise and lust. Israel survives the sorcerer's curse only to fall to the temptress's smile.

The people join themselves to Baal of Peor, eating at idol feasts and committing immorality, until the wrath of God breaks out in a plague. Paul holds this very episode before the Corinthian church: “We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day” (1 Cor 10:8). The point is unmistakable: a people who survived Egypt, the wilderness, and Balaam's curse can still be destroyed by their own appetites. Keller often warned that the church is rarely defeated by external persecution; far more often she is hollowed out by accommodation to the world's sensuality and idolatry. The danger is not the curse outside but the compromise within.

The chapter turns on the zeal of Phinehas, who, when an Israelite brazenly brings a Midianite woman into the camp, takes a spear and drives it through them both, and the plague is stopped. God commends his action and grants him “a covenant of peace” and “a covenant of perpetual priesthood,” because “he was jealous with my jealousy.” Ferguson notes that Phinehas's zeal is not bloodthirsty cruelty but holy jealousy that reflects God's own — a jealousy for the purity of God's people. His act of turning away wrath foreshadows the priestly work of Christ, the truly zealous One, who said “zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17), and who turns away the wrath of God from his people forever, not by another's death but by his own.

sections.title: Israel's Immorality and Idolatry at Peor
sections.commentary:
At Shittim, on the very threshold of the Promised Land, the men of Israel begin to commit immorality with Moabite women, who invite them to the sacrifices of their gods. Israel eats at the idol feasts and bows to Baal of Peor, yoking themselves to a false god. Keller observed that the gravest danger to the people of God is not the curse from without but the seduction within; what no sorcerer could do, lust and idolatry accomplish.

The placement is devastating: immediately after the glorious oracles of blessing, Israel plunges into shameful sin. The enemy who could not curse them found a way to corrupt them. The lesson stands: spiritual victory is no guarantee against the next temptation.

sections.title: The Wrath of God Kindled
sections.commentary:
The anger of the LORD is kindled, and a plague breaks out. Moses orders the judges to deal with those who joined Baal of Peor. In the midst of the weeping at the tent of meeting, a man of Israel brazenly brings a Midianite woman before the whole congregation. The plague rages until twenty-four thousand fall. Paul cites this very judgment as a warning to the church against sexual immorality (1 Cor 10:8).

The scale of the judgment is sobering. A people delivered through the sea and the wilderness, blessed by Balaam's oracles, now die by the thousands through their own sensuality. Sin within the camp is deadlier than any enemy without.

sections.title: The Zeal of Phinehas
sections.commentary:
Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, rises with a spear and runs the offending couple through, and the plague is stopped. God commends him: he “was jealous with my jealousy,” and so turned away God's wrath. God grants him a covenant of peace and perpetual priesthood. Ferguson notes that this is not mere violence but holy jealousy mirroring God's own zeal for the purity of his people; Phinehas stands in the breach as a true priest.

His act of turning away wrath foreshadows the priestly work of Christ, the truly zealous One (John 2:17), who turns away the wrath of God from his people — not by the death of the guilty, but by his own atoning death. Phinehas's covenant of peace points to the eternal covenant secured by the great High Priest.

sections.title: Judgment on Midian Announced
sections.commentary:
The slain man and woman are named, marking the public scandal, and God commands hostility against the Midianites, who had deliberately seduced Israel into the sin of Peor. The judgment to come on Midian (ch. 31) is announced here. Wenham notes that those who lead God's people into sin bear grave guilt; the seducers are held accountable.

The chapter ends with the principle that the deliberate corruption of God's people invites God's judgment on the corrupters. Yet the abiding lesson for Israel, and for the church, is the call to holy vigilance: to be jealous, as God is jealous, for the purity of his people, and to flee the seductions that no external enemy could ever impose from without.

25.theology:
Seduction from within. What Balaam's curse could not do, immorality and idolatry accomplished. The church is rarely defeated from without but often hollowed out by compromise within (1 Cor 10:8).

Holy jealousy. Phinehas was jealous with God's jealousy for the purity of his people. True zeal reflects God's own passion for holiness, not human cruelty.

Turning away wrath. Phinehas stood in the breach and stopped the plague, foreshadowing Christ the zealous Priest who turns away God's wrath by his own atoning death.
25.examples:
Then: Israel, unable to be cursed, was seduced into immorality and idolatry at Peor; the plague raged until Phinehas's holy zeal turned away God's wrath.

Now: Beware the seduction Balaam's curse could not achieve. The world will try to corrupt by pleasure what it cannot defeat by force. Flee sexual immorality and idolatry, and rest in Christ, the zealous Priest who turns God's wrath away forever.

26.title: The Second Census: A New Generation, an Old Faithfulness
26.text: <sup>63</sup>These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. <sup>64</sup>But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. <sup>65</sup>...not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
26.overview:
A second census bookends the book. Forty years after the first counting at Sinai, a new generation is numbered on the plains of Moab, poised once more at the edge of the Promised Land. The juxtaposition is breathtaking. The first census numbered the generation that would die in the wilderness for their unbelief; this one numbers the generation that will enter the land. The whole tragic interval of chapters 11–25 lies between the two countings.

The most moving verses are the closing ones (vv. 64–65): “among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron… not one of them was left, except Caleb… and Joshua.” The sentence of chapter 14 has been fully carried out. An entire generation — over 600,000 men — has died in the desert, just as God said. The wages of unbelief have been paid in full. Yet here is the staggering grace: God did not abandon the project. He did not give up on Israel. He raised up a new generation and brought them, against every odd, back to the border of promise. Sproul observed that here we see both the severity and the kindness of God (Rom 11:22): severity toward the unbelieving generation, kindness toward the new one. The promise outlived the failure.

This is the great comfort of the chapter: God's faithfulness spans the generations. The covenant did not die with the rebels in the sand. What God promised to Abraham, he will perform, even if it means burying one generation and raising up another. Ferguson notes that the church too is carried forward across generations by the faithfulness of God, not the constancy of men. Every funeral in the wilderness was real, but so was every birth; and the same God who kept his word of judgment kept his word of promise. He is faithful to a thousand generations, and the inheritance he pledged will surely be given, for it rests on him and not on us.

sections.title: The Command to Number the New Generation
sections.commentary:
After the plague, God commands Moses and Eleazar to take a census of all Israel twenty years and older, those able to go to war, on the plains of Moab. A new generation is mustered for the conquest that the old generation forfeited. Begg notes the symbolism of a fresh counting at the border: God is beginning again, preparing a people who will believe and enter where their parents would not.

The census is for war and for inheritance. These are the ones who will cross the Jordan and receive the land. The God who counts his people by name (ch. 1) counts again, knowing each member of the new generation he will bring home.

sections.title: The Tribes Counted Again
sections.commentary:
Tribe by tribe the new generation is numbered, totaling 601,730 — remarkably close to the first census, despite forty years of death and judgment. The note about the sons of Korah (v. 11) — “the sons of Korah did not die” — is a quiet shaft of grace: the rebel's line was preserved, and would later give Israel some of its most beautiful psalms. Wenham notes that God's mercy reaches even into the family of the great rebel.

The near-identical total testifies to God's faithfulness: he replaced the fallen generation man for man. Not one promise failed. The God who buried 600,000 also raised up 600,000, keeping his covenant across the chasm of judgment.

sections.title: Inheritance by Lot
sections.commentary:
God directs that the land be divided as an inheritance according to the size of each tribe, the portions assigned by lot. The larger tribes receive more, the smaller less, yet all by the casting of the lot, whose “every decision is from the LORD” (Prov 16:33). Ferguson notes that the inheritance is both ordered by human numbering and governed by divine sovereignty; God superintends the lot.

The land is gift and inheritance, distributed by God's hand. So the eternal inheritance is apportioned by God to his people, each given a place in the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.

sections.title: Not One Left of the Old Generation
sections.commentary:
The Levites are numbered separately, and then comes the solemn conclusion: of all those counted at Sinai, not one remained except Caleb and Joshua. The sentence of chapter 14 has been fully executed; the unbelieving generation has died to a man. Sproul saw here both the severity and the kindness of God (Rom 11:22): judgment fully carried out, yet a new people brought to the brink of promise.

The grace is overwhelming. God did not abandon his people but raised up a new generation and kept his covenant. The promise outlived the failure. God's faithfulness spans the generations; what he pledged to Abraham he will perform, for the inheritance rests on him and not on us.

26.theology:
God's faithfulness across generations. The covenant did not die with the unbelieving generation. God raised up a new people and kept his promise, faithful to a thousand generations.

Severity and kindness. Both are displayed (Rom 11:22): judgment fully carried out on the rebels, kindness extended to the new generation brought to the border of promise.

Grace in unexpected places. The sons of Korah did not die; the rebel's line was preserved to sing God's praises, a token of mercy reaching even into the family of judgment.
26.examples:
Then: A new generation was numbered at the border, nearly matching the first, while not one of the unbelieving generation remained except Caleb and Joshua.

Now: God's promises outlive every failure and span every generation. He buries one generation and raises another, never abandoning his covenant. The inheritance is sure because it rests on his faithfulness, not yours. Behold the severity and the kindness of God.

27.title: The Daughters of Zelophehad; Joshua Commissioned
27.text: <sup>7</sup>The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them. <sup>18</sup>So the LORD said to Moses, Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 holds two stories that, at first, seem unrelated: a daughters' appeal for inheritance, and the commissioning of Israel's next leader. But both turn on the same theme — the future of the people of God, the securing of the inheritance and the leadership that will bring them into it. As the new generation prepares to enter Canaan, God settles both who will inherit and who will lead.

The daughters of Zelophehad come forward with a bold and righteous appeal. Their father died without sons, and under the prevailing custom his name and inheritance would vanish. So five women stand before Moses, the priest, and the whole congregation and ask for their father's inheritance. It is a stunning act of courage and faith — faith, indeed, in the very promise of the land they have not yet entered. And God's verdict is striking: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right.” Wenham notes the dignity God grants these women; their claim is honored, the law is amended to provide for them, and the value of every person before God is upheld. Far from being marginalized, they are vindicated by the Lord himself. Their faith that God would surely give the land was so certain that they staked their future on it.

Then God turns to the matter of succession. Moses is told to go up the mountain and see the land — but, because of his sin at Meribah, he will not enter it. The pathos is deep: the great leader who endured forty years of grumbling will glimpse the land from afar but die outside it. Yet Moses' final concern is not for himself but for the people — “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (v. 17). So God appoints Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit,” and Moses lays his hands on him. Ferguson notes the gospel resonance: the shepherd's heart of Moses, and the name Joshua — Yeshua, the Hebrew form of “Jesus.” The Joshua who would lead the people into the earthly rest points to the greater Joshua, Jesus, who leads his people into the true and eternal rest that Moses, and the law, could never give (Heb 4:8–9).

sections.title: The Daughters' Bold Appeal
sections.commentary:
The five daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — stand before Moses and the whole assembly to plead that their father's name and inheritance not be lost because he had no sons. Their appeal is courageous, respectful, and rooted in faith that God will indeed give the land. Begg notes the boldness of their faith: they stake their claim on an inheritance not yet possessed, so sure are they of God's promise.

Far from presumption, their request honors the promise of God and the dignity of their father's name. They come not in rebellion but in faith, trusting that the God who promised the land will deal justly with his people.

sections.title: God Vindicates Their Claim
sections.commentary:
Moses brings their case before the LORD, and God's verdict is clear: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right.” The inheritance is to pass to them, and a permanent statute is established for such cases. Wenham notes the dignity God confers on these women and the justice of his law; their faith and courage are honored, not dismissed. The value of every person and the security of the inheritance are upheld by God himself.

This is a quiet but profound testimony to the heart of God toward the overlooked. He hears the appeal of the vulnerable and vindicates the faithful. In the kingdom of God, the inheritance is not finally a matter of human custom but of divine grace, secured for all who belong to him.

sections.title: Moses Shown the Land
sections.commentary:
God tells Moses to go up the mountain to see the land Israel will inherit, but reminds him that, because of his rebellion at the waters of Meribah, he will not enter it but will be gathered to his people like Aaron. The pathos is profound: the great mediator who bore the people for forty years will only glimpse the promise from afar. Sproul reflected that even the greatest servants of God are not above his discipline; Moses' sin had real consequences.

Yet there is grace even here. Moses sees the land, and his death is a gathering “to his people.” The law-giver cannot bring the people into rest; that points beyond him to another. Moses on the mountain, gazing at a land he cannot enter, reveals the limit of the law and the need for a greater Leader.

sections.title: Joshua Commissioned
sections.commentary:
Moses' final concern is not for himself but for the flock: that they not be “as sheep that have no shepherd.” God appoints Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit,” and Moses lays hands on him, conferring authority before Eleazar and the congregation. Ferguson notes the shepherd-heart of Moses and the resonance of the name: Joshua is Yeshua, the Hebrew form of Jesus.

The Joshua who leads Israel into the earthly land points to the greater Joshua, the Lord Jesus, who leads his people into the true rest the law could never secure (Heb 4:8–9). The Spirit-filled successor, commissioned by the laying on of hands, foreshadows the One anointed by the Spirit without measure, the Good Shepherd who will never leave his sheep without a shepherd.

27.theology:
God hears the faithful appeal. The daughters of Zelophehad, bold in faith, are vindicated by God himself. He honors the overlooked and secures the inheritance for those who trust his promise.

The limit of the law. Moses sees the land but cannot enter it. The law-giver cannot bring the people into rest, pointing beyond himself to a greater Leader.

The greater Joshua. Spirit-filled Joshua leads Israel into the land, foreshadowing Jesus, who leads his people into the true and eternal rest (Heb 4:8–9).
27.examples:
Then: God vindicated the daughters' faithful appeal and secured their inheritance, then commissioned Spirit-filled Joshua to shepherd the people into the land Moses could only see from afar.

Now: God hears the bold faith of the overlooked and secures your inheritance in Christ. And the greater Joshua, Jesus, leads you into the eternal rest the law could never give. You will never be left as sheep without a shepherd.

28.title: The Continual Offerings: The Rhythm of Worship
28.text: <sup>3</sup>And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering. <sup>6</sup>It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
28.overview:
As the new generation prepares to enter the land, God renews the calendar of worship — the daily, weekly, monthly, and seasonal offerings that are to mark the rhythm of their life with him. Chapter 28 may read like a liturgical timetable, but beneath it lies a glorious truth: God means to be worshipped continually, woven into the very fabric of time. Morning and evening, week by week, season by season, the smoke of sacrifice was to rise without ceasing before the LORD.

The foundation is the “regular” or “continual” burnt offering: two lambs every single day, one in the morning and one at twilight, never interrupted. Calvin noted that this daily, unbroken sacrifice taught Israel that fellowship with God is not occasional but constant; the people were to begin and end each day at the altar. Worship was not a weekly event but the heartbeat of daily existence. Upon this daily foundation are layered the Sabbath offerings, the monthly new-moon offerings, and the great festival offerings — an ascending rhythm of devotion that filled the whole calendar with the worship of God.

The book of Hebrews gathers up all these endless offerings and shows their meaning: “Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Heb 10:11–12). The very endlessness of the daily offerings preached their insufficiency; they had to be repeated because they could never finish the work. But there is a deeper gospel note still: the continual offering points to the continual intercession of Christ, our Great High Priest, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Heb 7:25). MacArthur observed that the unceasing smoke of the morning and evening lamb is a shadow of the unceasing advocacy of Christ before the Father. Day and night, without interruption, our Mediator presents his finished sacrifice and pleads for his people. The altar never went cold, because the love of God never sleeps.

sections.title: The Daily Burnt Offering
sections.commentary:
God commands the regular burnt offering: two unblemished year-old lambs, one in the morning and one at twilight, every day without fail, with grain and drink offerings. Calvin noted that this unbroken daily sacrifice taught Israel that communion with God is constant, not occasional; each day was to begin and end at the altar. The smoke was never to cease rising before the LORD.

The “continual” offering anchors all the rest. It is the steady heartbeat of Israel's worship, a shadow of the unceasing intercession of Christ who always lives to plead for us (Heb 7:25). The altar never went cold, because God means to be worshipped without interruption and to keep his people in constant fellowship with himself.

sections.title: The Sabbath Offering
sections.commentary:
On the Sabbath, the daily offering is doubled: two additional lambs with their grain and drink offerings. The day of rest is marked by increased worship, not diminished devotion. Begg notes that Sabbath rest and Sabbath worship belong together; ceasing from labor is for the sake of communion with God. The rhythm of work and rest is crowned by the rhythm of worship.

The doubled Sabbath offering points to the fuller rest and worship found in Christ, our true Sabbath, in whom we cease from our works and rest in his finished sacrifice (Heb 4:9–10). The weekly intensifying of worship anticipates the gathered worship of the church on the Lord's Day.

sections.title: The Monthly New-Moon Offering
sections.commentary:
At the beginning of each month, a generous offering of bulls, a ram, lambs, and a goat for a sin offering marks the new moon. The turning of every month is consecrated to God. Wenham notes the comprehensiveness: God claims not only days and weeks but months, sanctifying the whole calendar. Time itself is made holy by being offered to the LORD.

The monthly offering, with its sin offering, reminds the people of their continual need for atonement even as they mark the seasons. All of time belongs to God and is to be filled with his worship, anticipating the day when his people will worship him from new moon to new moon and Sabbath to Sabbath (Isa 66:23).

sections.title: The Passover and Feast of Weeks Offerings
sections.commentary:
The great spring festivals are appointed: the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread, recalling the exodus, and the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) with its firstfruits, each with prescribed offerings. The redemptive history of Israel is built into the worship calendar, so that the people relive their salvation year by year. Ferguson notes that biblical worship is rooted in remembrance of God's saving acts.

These feasts find their fulfillment in Christ: he is our Passover, sacrificed for us (1 Cor 5:7), and the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20), and at Pentecost the Spirit was poured out. The whole festal calendar of Numbers is a tapestry of shadows whose substance is Christ, in whom every appointed feast finds its Yes.

28.theology:
Continual worship. The daily morning and evening offering taught that fellowship with God is constant, not occasional. Worship is to be the heartbeat of daily life, the altar never going cold.

The continual intercession of Christ. The unceasing offering foreshadows our Great High Priest who always lives to make intercession (Heb 7:25), pleading his finished sacrifice without interruption.

Time made holy. Day, week, month, and season are all consecrated to God. The whole calendar is filled with worship, anticipating eternal worship before the throne.
28.examples:
Then: Israel offered the continual morning and evening sacrifice, with added offerings for Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts, so that worship filled the whole calendar.

Now: The endless offerings that could never finish are fulfilled in Christ's one finished sacrifice and his unceasing intercession. Day and night your Mediator pleads for you. Let your life be a continual offering of worship to the God who never sleeps.

29.title: The Feasts of the Seventh Month: The Climax of the Worship Year
29.text: <sup>1</sup>On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets. <sup>11</sup>...besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 continues the festal calendar into the seventh month, the holiest and fullest month of Israel's worship year, crowded with sacred days: the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the great Feast of Booths. If chapter 28 established the daily rhythm, chapter 29 brings the calendar to its glorious climax. The sheer abundance of sacrifice in this month — hundreds of animals offered over its festivals — proclaims the lavishness of worship that God's redemption deserves.

At the center stands the Day of Atonement (vv. 7–11), the most solemn day of the year, when the people afflicted their souls and the high priest made atonement for the sins of the whole nation. Even here, in Numbers' summary of the offerings, there is the “sin offering of atonement” — the costly reminder that a sinful people can dwell with a holy God only through blood. The book of Hebrews lavishes attention on this day, showing that the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood that could never finally cleanse, until Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Heb 9:12).

The month ends with the Feast of Booths, the great harvest festival of joy, when Israel dwelt in temporary shelters to remember their wilderness pilgrimage. Over its seven days, an astonishing number of bulls were offered — seventy in all, which the rabbis took to represent the nations of the world. Ferguson and others note the missionary hint: even Israel's joy looked outward, anticipating the day when the nations would be gathered to worship the God of Israel. The whole sweep of the chapter — trumpets sounding, atonement made, harvest joy overflowing — points to the consummation, when the trumpet shall sound (1 Cor 15:52), atonement is complete in Christ, and the redeemed from every nation dwell forever in the booth of God's presence. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Rev 21:3). The worship year of Numbers is a rehearsal for eternity.

sections.title: The Feast of Trumpets
sections.commentary:
The seventh month opens with a holy convocation announced by the blowing of trumpets, a day of rest and special offerings. The trumpet blast summons the people to attention before God at the start of the holiest month. Begg notes that the trumpet is a call to wake and remember, to gather the people to their God. The sound pierces the ordinary and declares a sacred season.

The trumpet of this feast echoes forward to the last trumpet, when Christ returns and the dead are raised (1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16). Every blast over Israel was a small foreshadowing of that great and final summons, when God will gather his people to himself forever.

sections.title: The Day of Atonement
sections.commentary:
On the tenth day, the people afflict themselves and do no work, while the prescribed offerings, including the “sin offering of atonement,” are made. This is the most solemn day of the year, when atonement is made for the sins of the whole nation. Sproul stressed the weight of this day: only through blood could a sinful people remain before a holy God. The afflicting of the soul taught Israel the gravity of sin.

Hebrews shows the fulfillment: the high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood that could never finally cleanse, until Christ entered once for all with his own blood, securing eternal redemption (Heb 9:12). The Day of Atonement is the shadow; the cross is the substance, where our great High Priest made atonement once for all.

sections.title: The Feast of Booths
sections.commentary:
The fifteenth day begins the seven-day Feast of Booths, the great harvest festival of joy, when Israel dwelt in temporary shelters remembering their wilderness pilgrimage. Over the week an enormous number of bulls is offered — seventy in all. Ferguson and others note the rabbinic reading that the seventy bulls represent the seventy nations, hinting at God's heart for the world even in Israel's feast.

The booths recall that God's people are pilgrims, dwelling in temporary shelters on the way to a permanent home. The joy of harvest anticipates the great ingathering, when the redeemed from every nation will dwell forever in the presence of God. Even Israel's celebration looked outward and forward to the consummation of all things in Christ.

sections.title: The Solemn Assembly
sections.commentary:
An eighth day, a solemn assembly, closes the festal season with a final set of offerings. The worship year reaches its consummation in a day of holy gathering and rest. It was on the great last day of this feast that Jesus stood and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), offering himself as the fulfillment of all the feast pointed toward. Wenham notes the fitting climax: the calendar ends in assembly and joy.

The whole sweep of the seventh month — trumpets, atonement, booths, solemn assembly — points to the consummation: the last trumpet, atonement complete in Christ, and the redeemed of every nation gathered to dwell forever in the booth of God's presence (Rev 21:3).
